terms.gloss: a fit of temper, a tantrum; also a quick temper
evidence: Sen. Ira 2.21.8: Nihil per īrācundiam exōret
terms.comment: Seneca’s word for the temper of a child who tries to get his way by it. Cicero separates īrācundia, the temper, from īra, the anger itself (Tusc. 4.27, Lewis & Short).

evidence: Cic. Verr. 2.2.48: exarsit īrācundiā ac stomachō

phrases.latin: Nihil per īrācundiam exōret: quod flentī negātum fuerit quiētō offerātur.
phrases.english: Let him get nothing by a tantrum: what was refused him while he cried should be offered him when he is calm.

phrases.latin: Plōrandō nihil impetrābis; ubi quiētus eris, vidēbimus.
phrases.english: Crying won’t get you anything; when you’re calm, we’ll see.

phrases.latin: Quantā īrācundiā exarsit, cum domum redīre jubērētur!
phrases.english: What a tantrum he threw when he was told to go home!

sources: Lewis & Short: iracundia · Lewis & Short: exardesco
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 392.
